svg.title: Four radioiodine trials answering two different questions
svg.desc: Schematic drawing four randomised radioiodine trials as two separate blocks, divided by a dashed rule labelled "Between the two questions: no arrow", because they answer two different questions. The first block is headed "Question one: whether to give radioiodine at all" and holds ESTIMABL2 and IoN. Its note says both are non-inferiority trials with the margin agreed in advance at five percentage points, and that a non-inferiority trial cannot show that something does not work - what it can say is "not worse". The ESTIMABL2 (France) card: randomised to radioiodine or none, 776 patients, all after total thyroidectomy. The event-free rate at three years was 95.6% with no radioiodine against 95.9% with it; at five years, with 698 patients evaluable, 93.2% against 94.8%. Both time points fall within the non-inferiority margin. The card notes that an "event" here is a composite - abnormal imaging or ultrasound, or a rise in thyroglobulin or antibodies - and is not recurrence and certainly not survival. Inside that card sits a second, red-bordered box headed "Who it excluded: this belongs in the same sentence as its conclusion", listing three exclusions: solitary papillary microcarcinoma of 1 cm or under, excluded outright, the trial's own stated reason being that ablation is not necessary in these patients; all node-positive disease; and pT2 and above. The box closes by recording what was enrolled - multifocal disease totalling one to two centimetres, or a solitary tumour of one to two centimetres, node-negative or not assessed - and states that the "low risk" this trial tested is not the low risk printed on a reader's report. The IoN (United Kingdom) card: also randomised to radioiodine or none, 33 centres, 504 patients, median follow-up 6.8 and 6.6 years. The crude recurrence-free rates at five years were 97.9% (96.1 to 99.7) with no radioiodine against 96.3% (93.9 to 98.7) with it, and the trial separately estimates a five-year absolute risk difference of 0.5 percentage points (95% confidence interval minus 2.2 to 3.2). The card states that the 0.5 is not those two rates subtracted: it is a separately estimated quantity, signed as the excess risk carried by leaving ablation out, and non-inferiority is declared because the top of that interval, 3.2, sits under the 5-point margin fixed in advance; subtract the two rates and you get 1.6 points, pointing the other way; and how the 0.5 was estimated cannot be said here, because the paper's methods section was not obtainable. Non-inferiority was met here too. Its endpoint differs from ESTIMABL2's: local recurrence or residual structural disease, distant metastasis and death from thyroid cancer counted together, with only 17 recurrences in the whole trial. The paper says it is still in follow-up, and the authors' conclusion is narrower than the entry criteria: pT1, pT2, node-negative or not assessed, with no adverse features. The lower half of that card is a small table headed "Inside the trial, the higher-risk patients really were at higher risk": of 46 patients with pT3 disease 4 recurred (9%); of 458 with pT1 or pT2, 13 (3%); of 47 with positive central nodes, 6 recurred (13%); and of 457 node-negative or not assessed, 11 (2%). The card closes by noting that the paper's next sentence is that these rates were similar in the patients who had no radioiodine, and that with only 17 events in the entire trial a subgroup in which no difference can be seen is not a subgroup in which there is none - this is "cannot be seen", not "shown not to exist". The second block is headed "Question two: how much to give" and holds HiLo and ESTIMABL1. Its note says every patient in these two trials received radioiodine, that what was randomised was the activity and the preparation, and that they say nothing whatever about whether to give it. The HiLo (United Kingdom) card: every patient received radioiodine, with a low activity of 1.1 and a higher activity of 3.7 GBq - the identifying feature of these two trials and nobody's prescription. The primary endpoint, the remnant cleared at six to nine months after treatment, was met in 85.0% on the low activity against 88.9% on the high activity; at a median follow-up of 6.5 years the cumulative recurrence at seven years was 5.9% against 7.3%, hazard ratio 1.10 (95% confidence interval 0.47 to 2.59). The card notes that the primary endpoint is a surrogate, not recurrence and not survival, and closes by saying that how much you yourself receive follows the rules of your hospital's nuclear medicine department. The ESTIMABL1 (France) card: again every patient received radioiodine, with the low activity of 1.1 randomised against the higher activity of 3.7 GBq together with the preparation, and again the primary endpoint was whether the remnant was cleared six to nine months after treatment. It closes by saying that using these trials to answer "whether" is running the two questions together. Below both blocks comes the point of the figure: inside one guideline, the strengths run in a counter-intuitive order. The introduction records that the 2025 edition divides recurrence risk into four tiers each carrying a probability - low, under 10%; low-intermediate, 10 to 15%; intermediate-high, 16 to 30%; and high, over 30% - and that those four percentages are probabilities of structural or biochemical recurrence, not mortality and not stage. Four rows follow, each giving the tier, the recommendation, the strength and the certainty. Low, under 10%: do not give routinely, strong recommendation, high certainty - this row is drawn with a heavy border. Low-intermediate, 10 to 15%, and intermediate-high, 16 to 30%: may be considered, conditional recommendation, low certainty. High, over 30%: give routinely, strong recommendation, moderate certainty. Distant metastases present at diagnosis: give, strong recommendation, moderate certainty. A yellow banner reads: set out in order it is plain, the hardest evidence is the evidence for not giving it. It adds that the guideline explains its own weakness in the middle tiers - too few studies look at those two tiers on their own - and that a systematic review lays it out further though it counts a different set of people - the middle box of the older three-tier stratification - with 11 observational studies seeing a benefit and 13 not, its authors adding that only a few of them had properly stratified populations, the boundaries having been redrawn since so that middle is not today's two middle boxes, while the shape of the disagreement has not changed. A further block records the European consensus: the 2022 European Thyroid Association consensus likewise lists high risk and known structural disease as indications, and not one of its recommendations carries a strength or a grade; it gives the reason low risk is hard to prove, namely that these patients have under a 1% chance of dying of thyroid cancer and only a 2% to 3% chance of persistence or recurrence, so a retrospective study can hardly demonstrate a benefit against a base rate like that; and it adds one line specifically about microcarcinoma, that papillary microcarcinoma of 1 cm or under with no other high-risk features should not be ablated, a line that applies to 1 cm and under and cannot be carried upward to tumours of one to four centimetres. The figure ends with a red-bordered block headed "This figure will not string the four trials together", holding five statements. The two blocks answer two different questions, so folding all four into "these four show radioiodine can be cut back" is wrong. The 1.1 and 3.7 GBq on this figure are the identifying feature of those two trials and nobody's prescription, and how much you receive, how you are prepared and whether you are admitted all follow the rules of your hospital's nuclear medicine department. ESTIMABL2's "low risk" always travels with its exclusions, and if the "low risk" on your report is not that cell then that conclusion was not made for you. On survival, no randomised trial has been run with overall survival as its primary endpoint (IoN's composite endpoint counts death from thyroid cancer, which is not overall survival): pooling the two trials, 1,280 patients in all, gives a hazard ratio for recurrence-free survival of 0.96 (0.80 to 1.15) and all-cause death 1.28 (0.48 to 3.41), intervals wide enough to straddle 1, which says "no difference is visible" and not "equally safe". And in 2017 the two nuclear medicine societies and the two thyroid associations, European and American, set up an intersocietal working group on the radioiodine controversy whose 2020 progress report states that the available evidence was insufficient to provide any definitive guidance and that they could not arrive at a consensus - if four societies cannot agree, two doctors giving you two answers is normal.

g.text: FOUR TRIALS, TWO DIFFERENT QUESTIONS
Four trials, two
questions: whether to
give it, and how much to
give
The four trials are often strung together as "all four
show radioiodine can be cut back". They cannot be.
They answer two different questions, so this figure
draws them as two blocks with a dashed rule between
them and no arrow.
In the first block, patients were randomised between
having radioiodine and not having it. In the second
block, every single patient received radioiodine.
Question one: whether to give radioiodine
at all
ESTIMABL2 and IoN. Both are non-inferiority trials, and both set the
margin agreed in advance at five percentage points. A
non-inferiority trial cannot show that something does not work; what
it can say is "not worse".
ESTIMABL2 (France)
Randomised: radioiodine, or none
776 patients, all after total thyroidectomy
Event-free rate at three years
none 95.6% / radioiodine 95.9%
At five years (698 evaluable)
none 93.2% / radioiodine 94.8%
Both time points fall within the non-inferiority margin. An "event"
here is a composite: abnormal imaging or ultrasound, or a rise in
thyroglobulin or antibodies. It is not recurrence, and it is certainly
not survival.
Who it excluded: this belongs in the same sentence as its
conclusion
Solitary papillary microcarcinoma of 1 cm or under was
excluded outright. The trial's own stated reason is that
ablation is not necessary in these patients.
All node-positive disease was excluded.
pT2 and above was excluded.
What was enrolled: multifocal disease totalling one to two
centimetres, or a solitary tumour of one to two centimetres,
node-negative or not assessed. So the "low risk" this trial
tested is not the low risk printed on a reader's report.
IoN (United Kingdom)
Randomised: radioiodine, or none
33 centres, 504 patients, median follow-up 6.8 and 6.6 years
Crude recurrence-free rates at five years
none 97.9% (96.1 to 99.7) / radioiodine 96.3% (93.9 to
Five-year absolute risk difference, estimated separately
0.5 percentage points (95% confidence interval −2.2
The figure the trial reports is not those two rates subtracted. The
0.5 is a separately estimated quantity, signed as the excess risk
carried by leaving ablation out, and non-inferiority is declared
because the top of that interval, 3.2, sits under the 5-point margin
fixed in advance; subtract the two rates and you get 1.6 points,
pointing the other way. How the 0.5 was estimated cannot be said
here: the paper's methods section was not obtainable.
Non-inferiority was met here too. Its endpoint differs from
ESTIMABL2's: local recurrence or residual structural disease,
distant metastasis and death from thyroid cancer counted together,
with only 17 recurrences in the whole trial. The paper says it is still
in follow-up, and the authors' conclusion is narrower than their
entry criteria - pT1, pT2, node-negative or not assessed, and no
adverse features.
Inside the trial, the higher-risk patients really were at higher risk
pT3 (46 patients)
4 recurrences, 9%
pT1 or pT2 (458 patients)
13 recurrences, 3%
Central nodes positive (47 patients)
6 recurrences, 13%
Negative or not assessed (457 patients)
11 recurrences, 2%
The paper's next sentence is that these rates were similar in the
patients who had no radioiodine. With only 17 events in the entire
trial, a subgroup in which no difference can be seen is not a
subgroup in which there is none. This is "cannot be seen", not
"shown not to exist".
Between the two questions: no arrow
Question two: how much to give
HiLo and ESTIMABL1. Every patient in these two trials received
radioiodine; what was randomised was the activity and the
preparation. They say nothing whatever about whether to give it.
HiLo (United Kingdom)
Randomised: activity, and preparation
Every patient received radioiodine. The low activity was 1.1 and the
higher activity 3.7 GBq - the identifying feature of these two trials,
and nobody's prescription.
Primary endpoint: remnant cleared at six to nine months after
treatment
low activity 85.0% / high activity 88.9%
Cumulative recurrence at seven years, median follow-up 6.5 years
5.9% against 7.3%
Hazard ratio
1.10 (95% confidence interval 0.47 to 2.59)
The primary endpoint is a surrogate: whether the remnant was
cleared. Not recurrence, and not survival.
As for how much you yourself receive: that follows the rules of
your hospital's nuclear medicine department.
ESTIMABL1 (France)
Randomised: activity, and preparation
Again every patient received radioiodine; what was randomised
was the low activity of 1.1 against the higher activity of 3.7 GBq, and
the preparation.
Primary endpoint
again whether the remnant was cleared six to nine
months after treatment
So both trials in this block ask what to give once the decision to give
it has already been made.
Using them to answer "whether" is running the two questions
together.
Inside one guideline, the strengths run in a
counter-intuitive order
The 2025 edition divides recurrence risk into four tiers, each carrying a
probability: low (under 10%), low-intermediate (10 to 15%),
intermediate-high (16 to 30%) and high (over 30%). Those four percentages
are probabilities of structural or biochemical recurrence - not mortality,
and not stage.
Low (under 10%)
Do not give routinely
Strong recommendation
high certainty
Low-intermediate (10 to 15%) and intermediate-high (16 to 30%)
May be considered
Conditional recommendation
low certainty
High (over 30%)
Give routinely
Strong recommendation
moderate certainty
Distant metastases present at diagnosis
Give
Strong recommendation
moderate certainty
Set out in order it is plain: the hardest evidence is the
evidence for NOT giving it
The guideline explains its own weakness in the middle tiers:
too few studies look at those two tiers on their own. A
systematic review lays it out further, though it is counting a
different set of people - the middle box of the older three-tier
stratification: 11 observational studies saw a benefit and 13
did not, and its authors add that only a few of them had
properly stratified populations. The boundaries have been
redrawn since, and that middle is not today's two middle
boxes; the shape of the disagreement has not changed.
The European consensus: the same direction, but no strength on any
line
The 2022 European Thyroid Association consensus likewise lists
high risk and known structural disease as indications; not one of its
recommendations carries a strength or a grade.
It gives the reason low risk is hard to prove: these patients have
under a 1% chance of dying of thyroid cancer and only a 2% to 3%
chance of persistence or recurrence, and a retrospective study can
hardly demonstrate a benefit against a base rate like that.
It adds one line specifically about microcarcinoma: papillary
microcarcinoma of 1 cm or under with no other high-risk features
should not be ablated. That line applies to 1 cm and under; it cannot
be carried upward to tumours of one to four centimetres.
This figure will not string the four trials together
The two blocks answer two different questions. ESTIMABL2
and IoN ask whether to give radioiodine; HiLo and
ESTIMABL1 ask how much, and in those two trials every
single patient received it. Folding all four into "these four
show radioiodine can be cut back" is wrong.
The 1.1 and 3.7 GBq on this figure are the identifying feature
of those two trials and nobody's prescription. How much you
receive, how you are prepared and whether you are
admitted all follow the rules of your hospital's nuclear
medicine department.
ESTIMABL2's "low risk" always travels with its exclusions:
solitary microcarcinoma of 1 cm or under, all node-positive
disease and pT2 and above are none of them in it. If the "low
risk" on your report is not that cell, that conclusion was not
made for you.
On survival: no randomised trial has been run with overall
survival as its primary endpoint (IoN's composite endpoint
counts death from thyroid cancer, which is not overall
survival). Pooling the two trials, 1,280 patients in all, gives a
hazard ratio for recurrence-free survival of 0.96 (0.80 to
1.15) and all-cause death 1.28 (0.48 to 3.41) - intervals wide
enough to straddle 1. That says "no difference is visible". It
does not say "equally safe".
In 2017 the two nuclear medicine societies and the two
thyroid associations, European and American, set up an
intersocietal working group on the radioiodine controversy.
Their 2020 progress report states that the available
evidence was insufficient to provide any definitive guidance
and that they could not arrive at a consensus. If four
societies cannot agree, two doctors giving you two answers
is normal.
Schematic, redrawn from the 2022 primary report and 2025
five-year follow-up of ESTIMABL2, the 2025 report of IoN, the 2019
long-term results of HiLo, the 2012 report of ESTIMABL1, the 2025
American Thyroid Association guidelines for differentiated thyroid
cancer, the 2022 European Thyroid Association consensus
statement, the 2015 systematic review of remnant ablation in
low-risk disease, the 2025 pooled analysis of the two trials and the
2020 progress report of the intersocietal working group; not
reproduced from the figures of the original papers. The cohorts,
designs and endpoints of the underlying studies differ, so the data
points must not be compared directly.
